TFLOPS counts trillions of calculations a second. FP16, FP8 and FP4 are number formats that use 16, 8 and 4 bits per number. The fewer the bits, the more calculations a chip can do.

Sources216 sources for 38 chips

B200Nvidia · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Dense, no sparsity, derived from Nvidia’s HGX B200 board table (8 GPUs: 36 PFLOPS FP16/BF16 and 72 PFLOPS FP8 with sparsity, 72 PFLOPS FP4 dense). The higher-power GB200 NVL72 variant reaches 10,000 dense FP4 TFLOPS per GPU. HGX B200 baseboards carry 180 GB per GPU, under the 192 GB quoted for the chip. All three formats are supported and published. The HGX table carries FP4, FP8/FP6, INT8, FP16/BF16, TF32, FP32 and FP64 rows for the board.

B300 (GB300 NVL72)Nvidia · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Dense. Derived from Nvidia’s GB300 NVL72 table: 1,080 PFLOPS dense NVFP4, and 720 PFLOPS FP8/FP6 and 360 PFLOPS FP16/BF16 with sparsity, across 72 GPUs. On the HGX boards FP16 is unchanged from the B200, at 36 PFLOPS with sparsity across eight GPUs. The B300's gains over the B200 are in FP4 and in attention softmax throughput. This row is the NVL72 part. The HGX B300 baseboard is slower, at 108 PFLOPS dense FP4 across eight GPUs, or 13,500 per GPU. All three formats are supported and published.

Rubin (VR200)Nvidia · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Dense, from Nvidia’s Vera Rubin NVL72 table. Its Rubin GPU column gives 35 PFLOPS NVFP4 and 17.5 PFLOPS FP8/FP6 for training and 4 PFLOPS FP16/BF16, all marked dense. FP16 is well under half the FP8 rate on this part. Nvidia separately quotes 50 PFLOPS per GPU of NVFP4 inference with sparsity

H200 (China-licensed configuration)Nvidia · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Dense. Nvidia’s H200 SXM page quotes 1,979 TFLOPS BF16 and 3,958 TFLOPS FP8 with sparsity. The figures here are half of those. Hopper has no four-bit datapath. In its list of tensor-core types, Nvidia’s Hopper architecture post says “The FP8, FP16, BF16, TF32, FP64, and INT8 MMA data types are supported” and names no FP4. So the FP4 cell reads not supported.

H20 (HGX H20, China variant)Nvidia · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Dense, from Epoch AI’s hardware database, which records 148 TFLOPS FP16 and BF16 for the HGX H20. Nvidia has never published an H20 datasheet, and no allowed source gives a separate FP8 figure. FP8 is still supported, because the H20 is a cut-down Hopper part and Nvidia’s Hopper post lists FP8 among the supported tensor-core types. With no figure, the FP8 cell reads not published. Hopper has no four-bit datapath. In its list of tensor-core types, Nvidia’s Hopper architecture post says “The FP8, FP16, BF16, TF32, FP64, and INT8 MMA data types are supported” and names no FP4. So the FP4 cell reads not supported. Epoch AI describes the part as a slightly scaled-down H200 on every measure except arithmetic, where it reaches only about 15 percent of the H200.

H800 (China variant of the H100)Nvidia · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Dense, and identical to the H100. Epoch AI states that the H800 had exactly the same arithmetic performance as the H100 and records 989 TFLOPS dense FP16. The FP8 figure is the H100’s, halved from Nvidia’s sparse 3,958. Nvidia published no H800 datasheet outside China. Hopper has no four-bit datapath. In its list of tensor-core types, Nvidia’s Hopper architecture post says “The FP8, FP16, BF16, TF32, FP64, and INT8 MMA data types are supported” and names no FP4. So the FP4 cell reads not supported.

A800 (China variant of the A100)Nvidia · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Dense, and identical to the A100. CSIS describes the A800 as a modified A100 engineered to stay below the 600 GB/s interconnect limit, and Epoch AI’s hardware database records the same 312 TFLOPS dense FP16. Nvidia never published an A800 datasheet outside China, so no vendor figure exists. Ampere has neither an eight- nor a four-bit float datapath. Nvidia’s Ampere architecture post states that “Third-generation Tensor Cores add support for TF32, BF16, FP64, INT8, INT4, and binary data types”. So the FP8 and FP4 cells read not supported.

H100 (SXM5)Nvidia · United States

So the FP4 cell reads not supported.

A100 (80 GB SXM)Nvidia · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Dense. Nvidia’s A100 spec table gives 312 TFLOPS FP16 and BF16 tensor core and 624 TOPS INT8 for both the SXM and PCIe parts. Its doubled figures (624 TFLOPS and 1,248 TOPS) are marked with sparsity. Ampere has neither an eight- nor a four-bit float datapath. Nvidia’s Ampere architecture post states that “Third-generation Tensor Cores add support for TF32, BF16, FP64, INT8, INT4, and binary data types”. So the FP8 and FP4 cells read not supported.

Instinct MI355XAMD · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Dense matrix across 256 compute units, checked against AMD’s datasheet: FP16 and BF16 2.5166 PFLOPS, MXFP8 and OCP-FP8 5.0332, INT8 5.0332 POPS and MXFP4 10.0663 PFLOPS. Its structured-sparsity column doubles FP16, BF16, OCP-FP8 and INT8, and reads N/A for MXFP8, MXFP6 and MXFP4. All three formats are supported and published

Instinct MI455XAMD · United States

How the speed figures are measured. AMD’s datasheet gives these peak theoretical figures: 40,265 TFLOPS OCP MXFP4, 20,133 TFLOPS OCP MXFP6, MXFP8 and FP8, and 5,033 TFLOPS matrix FP16, BF16 and INT8. The datasheet’s separate structured-sparsity column doubles FP16, BF16 and INT8 to 10,066 TFLOPS and lists no sparsity figure for the MX formats or FP8. All three formats are supported and published.

Instinct MI325XAMD · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Dense, from AMD’s footnote MI325-002: 1,307.4 TFLOPS FP16, 1,307.4 TFLOPS BF16, 2,614.9 TFLOPS FP8 and 2,614.9 TOPS INT8. These match the MI300X, because the MI325X is the same CDNA 3 silicon with faster, larger memory. AMD’s sparsity column doubles each figure. CDNA 3 has no four-bit datapath. AMD’s CDNA 3 white paper tabulates every matrix type the architecture runs (Matrix FP64, FP32, TF32, FP16, BF16, FP8 and INT8), and the string FP4 appears nowhere in the document. So the FP4 cell reads not supported.

Instinct MI300XAMD · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Dense, from AMD’s own footnote MI300-17: 1,307.4 TFLOPS FP16, 1,307.4 TFLOPS BF16, 2,614.9 TFLOPS FP8 and 2,614.9 TOPS INT8 at 2,100 MHz across 304 compute units. The CDNA 3 white paper tabulates the same figures. AMD’s separate structured-sparsity column doubles each of those. CDNA 3 has no four-bit datapath. AMD’s CDNA 3 white paper tabulates every matrix type the architecture runs (Matrix FP64, FP32, TF32, FP16, BF16, FP8 and INT8), and the string FP4 appears nowhere in the document. So the FP4 cell reads not supported.

TPU v7 (Ironwood)Google · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Google’s Cloud TPU documentation gives peak per-chip compute of 2,307 TFLOPS BF16 and 4,614 TFLOPS FP8, the only two precisions the tpu7x table carries. These are dense. Google publishes no sparsity figures, and the four SparseCores are engines for embedding lookups. Four-bit arithmetic arrives with the next generation. Google’s eighth-generation deep dive says “TPU 8t introduces native 4-bit floating point (FP4)”, so the FP4 cell reads not supported.

TPU 8tGoogle · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Google publishes a 12.6 PFLOPS FP4 peak and no other precision for this part, and does not say whether it is dense or sparse. It says TPU 8t “introduces native 4-bit floating point (FP4)”, doubling the throughput of its matrix multiply units. It publishes no list of other formats, so the FP16 and FP8 cells read not published

TPU 8i (Zebrafish)Google · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Google publishes a 10.1 PFLOPS FP4 peak and no other precision for this part, and does not say whether it is dense or sparse. FP4 is the only format Google names for either eighth-generation chip, and it publishes no list of supported data types. Nothing shows whether the hardware carries FP16 and FP8 paths, so those cells read not published. Third-party FP8 and BF16 numbers in circulation are derived by halving and are not official.

  1. Google Cloud: TPU 8t and TPU 8i technical deep dive
  2. Google blog: eighth-generation TPUs for the agentic era

TPU v6e (Trillium)Google · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Google’s v6e documentation gives 918 TFLOPs peak bf16 per chip and 1,836 TOPs peak Int8, both dense, and lists no FP8 row. The eight-bit figure is INT8, so it stays in this note and out of the FP8 field. Two Google pages disagree about whether the part has an FP8 path at all. The tpu7x table prints “Peak compute per chip (FP8) (TFLOPs) … 918” for v6e, which is the bf16 figure repeated, with no gain in throughput. Nothing settles it, so the FP8 cell reads not published. No Google page gives v6e a four-bit rate, and Google dates native FP4 to the eighth generation, so the FP4 cell reads not supported.

TPU v5pGoogle · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Google’s v5p table gives 459 TFLOPs peak per chip for BF16 and the same 459 TFLOPs for FP8. Dropping to eight-bit gives no extra throughput on this part, unlike the Blackwell and CDNA generations. Google still prints the FP8 row, so the format is supported and published. Both figures are dense. Google publishes no sparsity numbers. No Google page gives the v5p a four-bit rate and Google dates native FP4 to the eighth generation, so the FP4 cell reads not supported. Capacity is quoted in GiB.

TPU v5eGoogle · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Google’s v5e table gives 197 TFLOPs peak bf16 per chip and 393 TOPs peak Int8, both dense, and no other precision. The eight-bit path is INT8, so eight-bit work on a v5e runs as integer quantization with no eight-bit floating-point path in hardware. The FP8 cell therefore reads not supported. No Google page gives this part a four-bit rate either, and Google dates native FP4 to the eighth generation. Google’s v5e table of May 2024 gave the memory as 16 GB of HBM2 at 819 GBps, and the memory fields above carry those figures. The current table names no HBM generation and lists the bandwidth as 800 GiBps.

TPU v4Google · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Google gives a single figure, “275 teraflops (bf16 or int8)” per chip, and names no other format. Eight-bit math runs no faster than bf16 on this part, and the eight-bit path is integer. There is no FP8 and no FP4 datapath, so both cells read not supported. Memory capacity is quoted as 32 GiB.

How the speed figures are measured. Dense, from the AWS Neuron architecture docs: eight NeuronCore-v3 deliver 1,299 FP8 TFLOPS, 667 BF16, FP16 and TF32 TFLOPS, and 181 FP32 TFLOPS, with 2,563 TFLOPS quoted for the sparse case. Maia 200Microsoft · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Microsoft’s architecture deep dive gives 10.1 PetaOPS FP4 and says FP4 throughput on Maia 200 is 2x that of FP8 and 8x that of BF16. That gives 5,050 TFLOPS FP8 and 1,263 TFLOPS BF16. Microsoft's launch post says “over 10 petaFLOPS” FP4 and “over 5 petaFLOPS” FP8. Epoch AI’s database uses the same arithmetic and records 1,268 TFLOPS BF16. All three formats are supported. Microsoft does not say whether the figures are dense or sparse, and publishes no separate tensor-core FP16 rate.

MTIA 400Meta · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Meta’s blog gives only ratios to MTIA 300: 400 percent higher FP8 FLOPS and 51 percent higher HBM bandwidth. It publishes no absolute figure for either part, so the ratios cannot be turned into numbers. Meta writes that MTIA 400 “supports enhanced versions of MX8 and MX4, which are important low-precision formats”, so the eight- and four-bit cells both read not published. It names no 16-bit rate or type for this generation. The absolute figures Meta showed at Hot Chips 2026 are in a deck that requires registration.

MTIA 300Meta · United States

How the speed figures are measured. From the spec table in Meta’s ISCA 2026 paper: 1,120 TFLOPS FP8 and 560 TFLOPS FP16/BF16. The paper does not say whether these are dense or sparse. It says MTIA 300 has no native datapath for four-bit formats such as MX4 and runs them in software instead, so the FP4 cell reads not supported. MTIA v2Meta · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Dense. Meta’s table gives 354 TOPS INT8 and 177 TFLOPS FP16 and BF16 for the matrix engines at 1.35 GHz, with 708 and 354 quoted for the sparse case. The vector core adds 11.06 TOPS INT8, 5.53 TFLOPS FP16 and 2.76 TFLOPS FP32. Apart from FP32 on the vector core, the table carries only INT8 and FP16/BF16. There is no FP8 and no FP4 datapath, so both cells read not supported.

JalapeñoOpenAI with Broadcom · United States

How the speed figures are measured. OpenAI publishes no per-precision FLOPS and argues that performance per unit of power is the more useful standard. SemiAnalysis gives 13.4 PFLOPS of MXFP4 for the B0 stepping (chip revision), a theoretical peak with no dense or sparse basis stated. OpenAI's own results show MXFP4 models running on the chip. FP16 and FP8 read not published. On SemiAnalysis’s InferenceX benchmark, OpenAI reports peak interactivity of 1,459 tokens per second per user on GPT-OSS 120B, 700 on DeepSeek R1 and 694 on Kimi K2.5.

Gaudi 3Intel · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Intel’s Gaudi 3 white paper gives 1,678 TFLOPS for both FP8 and BF16 on the matrix engines, in its comparison with Gaudi 2 and again in Table 5. Table 5 also lists 459 TFLOPS for FP16 (signed) and TF32, and 229 for FP32. Epoch AI records the same 1,678. Intel’s Gaudi documentation gives 1.8 PFLOPS for FP8 and BF16 across 8 matrix multiplication engines and 64 tensor processor cores on two compute dies. Neither Intel source says whether the figures are dense or sparse. Gaudi 3 has no four-bit datapath. The white paper states that “the Intel Gaudi 3 AI accelerator MME supports all the key AI compute datatypes: FP8 (both E4M3 and E5M2), BF16, FP16, TF32 and FP32” and never mentions FP4, so the FP4 cell reads not supported.

Gaudi 2Intel · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Intel publishes no Gaudi 2 datasheet of its own. Its Gaudi 3 white paper tabulates the two parts together and gives Gaudi 2's matrix engines (MME) 432 TFLOPS BF16 and 865 TFLOPS FP8, the figures shown above. WSE-3 Turbo (CS-4)Cerebras · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Cerebras quotes 250 PFLOPS of AI compute per WSE-3 Turbo, double the original WSE-3. It names no precision and no dense or sparse basis for the figure, so it fits none of the table's speed rows. Cerebras’s developer documentation says “The CS system offers support for the following data formats” and lists FP32, FP16, cbfloat16 and bfloat16. So FP16 is supported, with no published figure. But that page documents the training software for the CS platform and predates the CS-4. Cerebras publishes no data-type list for the WSE-3 Turbo, so the FP8 and FP4 cells read not published.

LPUGroq · United States

How the speed figures are measured. Derived from a rack figure. Groq quotes 315 PFLOPS of FP8 inference compute and 40 PB/s of SRAM bandwidth per 256-LPU rack, which works out to about 1,230 TFLOPS FP8 and 156 TB/s per accelerator. Groq does not say whether the figure is dense or sparse. FP16 is supported, but no current figure exists. Epoch AI records 188 TFLOPS FP16 and 750 TOPS INT8 for the first-generation GroqChip, from a Groq product brief whose link no longer works. Mixing that generation’s figures with a rack-derived FP8 figure would misstate the part, so the FP16 cell stays empty. Groq names no four-bit format anywhere, but publishes no data-type list either, so FP4 reads not published. Groq’s own LPU page puts on-chip SRAM bandwidth at “upwards of 80 terabytes per second”, roughly half the rack-derived figure. The two Groq pages disagree, and both are recorded here.

Ascend 910BHuawei (HiSilicon) · China

How the speed figures are measured. CSET puts the second-generation Ascend 910B series at a theoretical maximum of 400 TFLOPS FP16, 80 TFLOPS above the first-generation 910. CSET finds that only about 75 percent of that gain is real hardware. Half of the gain comes from a higher clock, a quarter from an extra vector unit per AI core, and the last quarter from a change in how Huawei counts peak performance. Huawei publishes no per-chip figure of its own. Its Atlas 800T A2 server gives 3.0 or 2.5 PFLOPS FP16 across eight NPUs, which is 375 or 312.5 TFLOPS per chip. Huawei’s own roadmap says eight- and four-bit floats arrive with the 950 series: “Compared with the Ascend 910B and Ascend 910C, our newer chips – starting with the Ascend 950 chips – … will support more data formats, including FP32, HF32, FP16, BF16, FP8, MXFP8, HiF8, MXFP4, and HiF4.” So the FP8 and FP4 cells read not supported.

Its Atlas 900 A3 SuperPoD page gives 307.2, 288.7 or 240.3 PFLOPS FP16 across 384 chips, depending on the model, which is 800, 752 or 626 TFLOPS per chip. MTT S5000Moore Threads · China

How the speed figures are measured. Moore Threads publishes no peak FLOPS for the MTT S5000. Its product page instead claims “full-precision compute support from FP8 to FP64” on the PH100 “Pinghu” chip. So FP16 and FP8 are supported, but no figures are published for them. No independent benchmark exists.
